passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, by Mrs D'Souza.
For weeks Shalini has been saying "I'm so dumb" after every answer, and today she refused to try out for the science quiz team. I watched her friend Alka handle it. Alka didn't say "Don't be silly." She said, "You explained the magnet question to me yesterday better than the textbook did." She kept sitting beside Shalini at lunch.
After school Alka brought Shalini to my desk and said, "She's been down for ages. I think she should talk to someone." I listened to Shalini for twenty minutes. With her agreement, I have told the school counsellor, and I will call her mother tonight.

qa.q: Which question had Shalini explained to Alka?
qa.a: She had explained the magnet question.

qa.q: What might Alka have been feeling when she brought Shalini to the teacher's desk?
qa.a: Alka seems worried about Shalini, since she says "She's been down for ages" and wants her to talk to someone.

qa.q: What choices did Alka make as a friend, and why were they wise?
qa.a: She gave honest, specific praise, stayed beside Shalini, and brought her to a trusted adult when the low mood lasted.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Alka says she should talk to someone?
qa.a: She may feel exposed at first, but also cared for, since Alka stayed with her and came along.

grounding: A teacher records how a teenager noticed a friend's constant put-downs, offered specific praise, stayed close and brought her to a trusted adult.

passage:
Friday night.
Lalit did it again at cricket nets. Dropped one catch and said "Useless, I'm always useless" three times, loudly. Then he said no to captaining the Under-16s, even though Coach asked him first. I don't get it. He's the only one who remembers everyone's birthdays. So I told him, not in a gushing way, "You read spin better than anyone. You got Sahil out twice last week." He shrugged, but he stopped muttering. I'm walking with him to nets every day next week. If he's still this down after the holidays, I'll ask if he wants to talk to his chacha, the one he actually listens to. Or I'll tell Coach.
Jahnavi

qa.q: What did Lalit say no to?
qa.a: He said no to captaining the Under-16s.

qa.q: What does Lalit's "I'm always useless" suggest he feels about himself?
qa.a: It suggests he feels worthless after small mistakes, even though he has real strengths.

qa.q: What choice did Jahnavi make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Jahnavi gave honest, specific praise about reading spin and getting Sahil out, and planned to walk with Lalit to nets, which gives him real evidence and company.

qa.q: How might Lalit's chacha help if Lalit stays down?
qa.a: As a trusted adult Lalit listens to, the chacha could hear him out and help him get more support.

grounding: A teenager notices a friend's put-downs and refusals, gives specific praise, stays close and plans to involve a trusted adult if the low mood lasts.

passage: On the way back from the tuition centre in Sitapur, Charu kicked the dust and said again, "I'm useless at everything." It was the fourth time that week Raghav had heard it. That afternoon she had refused the teacher's offer to present their water-filter model at the block science fair. "Let Raghav do it. I'll mess up." Raghav knew she'd built most of it. He stopped under the neem tree. "You worked out the charcoal layer. I didn't even know charcoal could clean water." She shrugged. He walked her home every day that week. On Friday, when she said she felt low all the time and wasn't sleeping, he said, "Let's tell Kamla-didi at the health centre, now. I'll come." That evening Kamla-didi sat with them on the bench outside the centre and listened.

qa.q: What did Charu refuse to present?
qa.a: Their water-filter model at the block science fair.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking when Charu said "Let Raghav do it"?
qa.a: He felt concerned and a little frustrated, knowing she'd built most of the model.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Taking her to Kamla-didi that same day, because her low mood had lasted and needed a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Raghav praises the charcoal layer?
qa.a: Charu might feel noticed but unable to believe it yet, which is why she shrugged.

grounding: Illustrates a friend hearing constant put-downs, giving specific praise, staying close and involving a trusted adult.

passage: Jamal had known Rania since they were nine, at the same Birmingham school. Lately she said "I'm so thick" after every answer, even right ones. When the art teacher offered her a place in the city exhibition, Rania said no before the teacher had finished the sentence. Jamal waited till they were at the bus stop. "The bird you painted, the one with the torn wing, people stopped in the corridor to look at it. I did too." Rania rolled her eyes, but she didn't change the subject. He sat with her at lunch every day that week, not fixing anything. On Friday he said, "You've seemed low for ages. Would you talk to Ms Okafor? I'll wait outside her door." Rania thought for a long moment, then nodded.

qa.q: What did Rania paint?
qa.a: A bird with a torn wing.

qa.q: What was Jamal feeling as he watched Rania turn down the exhibition?
qa.a: He was worried and sad, seeing her put herself down and miss a real chance.

qa.q: What did Jamal do that could help Rania?
qa.a: He gave specific praise, stayed close at lunch and encouraged her to talk to Ms Okafor, offering to wait outside.

qa.q: How might Rania see Jamal's offer to wait outside the door?
qa.a: She may feel supported and less scared, knowing she won't face the talk alone.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing low self-worth, sharing specific praise, staying close and encouraging a trusted adult.

passage:
In the school study hall, Sharmila crumpled another page. "I'm so stupid. I can't even write a paragraph."
Wasim looked up. It was the fourth time that week he'd heard her say it. On Monday she had turned down the chance to read her poem in assembly: "They'll laugh."
He leaned over. "Can I be honest? Your poem about your grandmother's hands is the best thing anyone wrote this term. The line about the turmeric stains, I still remember it."
Sharmila stared at the table. "You're just being nice."
"I'm being specific." He didn't leave. He sat with her till the bell.
As they packed up, he said quietly, "You've seemed down for weeks. Would you talk to Mrs Das? I'll come along."
She nodded. They walked to the staff room together, and Mrs Das made time to see her that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Sharmila turn down on Monday?
qa.a: The chance to read her poem in assembly.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel hearing Sharmila call herself stupid again?
qa.a: He was concerned, since it was the fourth time that week, and he chose to stay and offer honest praise.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that a good friend could copy?
qa.a: He gave specific, honest praise, stayed close until the bell, and gently encouraged her to talk to a trusted adult, even offering to go with her.

qa.q: Why might Sharmila say "You're just being nice"?
qa.a: Her low sense of worth makes praise hard to believe, so kind words feel fake to her, even specific ones.

grounding: Shows a friend who hears repeated put-downs, offers honest specific praise, stays close, and helps her reach a trusted adult.
